fix(auth/jwt): surface upstream JWT errors and log every auth failure

The handler previously matched only errors whose code started with
FST_JWT_, but fastify-jwt-jwks throws plain http-errors Unauthorized
instances (no code, just a statusCode and a descriptive message).
Those landed in the catch-all 'throw unauthorized()' branch, which
discarded the message and emitted no log line — so an expired or
malformed token surfaced to the client as a generic 401 and left
no trace on the server.

Forward any non-Boom error with statusCode < 500 as a Boom carrying
the original message, and log every non-Boom error at warn so the
underlying cause is always visible in server logs. Keep the generic
unauthorized() fallback for unknown server errors.

Fixes #757

fix(auth/jwt): log 5xx errors at error level with distinct message

In the previous commit every non-Boom error logged at warn with the
message 'JWT authentication failed', including the 5xx fallback path
(e.g. JWKS fetch failures) where the client receives 401 but the
underlying problem is a server-side fault. That under-reports severity
and misleads incident investigation.

Split into two log lines: 4xx errors stay at warn with the auth-failure
message; the 5xx fallback logs at error level with 'Unexpected error in
JWT handler'.

createWriteStream fire-and-forgot blockBlobClient.uploadStream, so pipeline() in

Artifact storage keys were built with the platform-dependent path.join,
so a cache server running on Windows produced keys like 'team\hash'
while Linux/macOS produced 'team/hash'. For remote stores (S3, GCS,
Azure) these are object keys, so artifacts cached on one OS could never
be resolved by a runner on another, defeating cross-platform cache reuse.

that always uses path.posix.join, and add a regression test.

fix(storage): surface backend failures as 5xx instead of masking as cache miss

GET/HEAD /artifacts returned 404 on any error from the storage layer,
because both the S3 provider's `exists` and the route handlers collapsed
every error into "not found". A real S3 failure (throttling, 5xx,
network) therefore looked like an ordinary cache miss, silently tanking
the cache hit rate and hiding the incident (the error was even logged at
`info` level) instead of surfacing as a 5xx.

- s3 `exists` now only treats a genuine missing object as a miss and
  propagates real backend errors. `isCacheMissError` classifies 404
  (NotFound/NoSuchKey) and 403 as misses -- S3 returns 403 for a missing
  object when the IAM policy lacks s3:ListBucket (least-privilege setups),
  so 403 must stay a miss or every miss would become a 5xx. Throttling,
  5xx, timeouts and connection errors propagate.
- The location layer rejects genuine not-found with a dedicated
  `ArtifactNotFoundError`; route handlers map only that to 404 and rethrow
  every other error so it surfaces as a 5xx.

Tests: unit coverage for `isCacheMissError` and a regression test that a
downed storage backend yields 5xx (not 404).

Closes #815

fix(storage): propagate Azure download failures instead of hanging the request

`createAzureBlobStorage().createReadStream()` called `blobClient.download()`
and handled only the fulfilled path. Three failure modes went unhandled:

- A rejected download produced an unhandled promise rejection. There is no
  `unhandledRejection` handler in `src/` and no `--unhandled-rejections`
  override, so on Node >= 15 this terminates the process.
- A response without `readableStreamBody` (the field is optional in the Azure
  types) left the PassThrough neither ended nor destroyed, so the request hung
  until timeout.
- `pipe()` does not forward errors, so a body failing partway through (dropped
  connection) also left the stream open.

All three now destroy the returned stream with the underlying error, so the
failure surfaces as a 5xx and is logged, matching what the S3 provider already
does in `storage/s3.ts`.

With AUTH_MODE=jwt, the server checked only the token scope. The team
came from the query string, so each valid token could read, write, and

fix(remote-cache): stream artifact uploads to storage instead of buffering full body in memory

The `application/octet-stream` content-type parser used `parseAs: 'buffer'`,
which loads the entire upload into the Node.js heap before `put-artifact`
re-wraps it with `Readable.from(req.body)` and pipes it to storage. Each
concurrent upload therefore holds up to `BODY_LIMIT` bytes in memory, so a burst
of large uploads can OOM the server even though every storage driver already
streams to the backend via `createWriteStream`.

Replace the buffering parser with a raw-stream passthrough and pipe the request
body straight into `createCachedArtifact`. `BODY_LIMIT` is still enforced: an
advertised `content-length` over the limit is rejected up front, and a
byte-counting transform inside the storage pipeline is the backstop for
chunked/unknown-length uploads — both return 413. The HTTP contract is
unchanged.

Closes #679

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(remote-cache): publish streamed artifacts atomically via a temporary key

Streaming uploads straight to the final storage key means the bytes that
arrive before a failure are already written. With the local provider that
leaves a truncated file at `<team>/<artifactId>`, which `exists` then reports
as a cache hit and `createReadStream` serves as a valid artifact — turning a
rejected upload into permanent cache corruption. Before this PR the body was
fully buffered and size-checked by fastify, so the write was all-or-nothing.

Restore that guarantee: `StorageProvider` gains optional `promote` and
`remove` hooks, the local adapter implements them (same-filesystem `rename`,
which is atomic), and `createCachedArtifact` streams into a sibling temporary
key and promotes it only once the whole body has landed. The temporary key is
removed on failure and the final key is deliberately left untouched, so a
failed overwrite cannot evict an artifact that is already cached.

Providers that cannot promote without re-transferring the payload (object
stores, where it costs a server-side copy plus a delete on every artifact)
opt out and keep writing directly to the final key.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(remote-cache): abort the S3 multipart upload when the write stream is destroyed

`pipeline()` destroys the destination writable when an upstream stage fails —
which is exactly what the BODY_LIMIT guard does on an oversized upload — and
destruction skips `final()`. The S3 adapter's writable only implemented
`write` and `final`, so on destroy the internal PassThrough feeding
@aws-sdk/lib-storage was never ended and `Upload.abort()` was never called:
parts already uploaded lingered in the bucket accruing storage cost until a
lifecycle rule reaped them, and the orphaned `upload.done()` promise could
reject with no handler attached and take the process down.

Implement `destroy()` to destroy the PassThrough and abort the upload, and
attach a handler to the upload promise at creation time. The abort is
fire-and-forget: it is a network round-trip to S3, and blocking the destroy
callback on it would stall `pipeline()` — and therefore the HTTP response —
until the remote cleanup returned.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(remote-cache): ignore a negative content-length in the body-limit fast path

`Number.isFinite(-1)` is true and `-1 > bodyLimit` is false, so a negative
advertised length silently skipped the fast path without comment. Require a
non-negative value so a meaningless content-length falls through to the
in-pipeline byte counter like any other unknown-length upload.

fix(remote-cache): abort the Azure block upload when the write stream is destroyed

pipeline() destroys the destination when an upstream stage fails, and
destruction skips final(). The Azure SDK BufferScheduler listens to the
data, end and error events of the stream only. Thus the upload promise
never settled, and its buffers stayed in memory for each failed upload.

The write stream now destroys the internal PassThrough with an error and
aborts the SDK request. A completed upload skips this step, because
autoDestroy also calls destroy() after a successful finish.

fix(remote-cache): fail the write stream when the storage upload fails

When a block upload (Azure) or an UploadPart request (S3) fails, the SDK
stops reading the internal PassThrough. A pending write then never called
back, so pipeline() stalled and the PUT request did not get a response.

The upload promise handler now destroys the write stream with the upload
error. The handler is attached at creation time, so no rejection is
unhandled. A second destroy() call on a destroyed stream does nothing, and
final() still reports a failure inside final() once. On S3, lib-storage
aborts the multipart upload before it rejects, so the adapter does not
send a second abort request.

fix(remote-cache): close the connection when an upload fails before the body ends

The Fastify body parser sends `connection: close` when the body fails,
because the client can send more data. The PUT route now reads the body
itself. When the upload failed before the body ended, pipeline() destroyed
the request, and the server stopped reading the socket. The response still
kept the connection alive. Thus the next request on that connection got no
response until the keep-alive timeout reset the socket.

The route now sets `connection: close` on HTTP/1 in these cases:
- The content-length check rejects the upload. Node then does not read the
  declared body.
- The upload fails before the request body is complete, with a 413 or a 412.
HTTP/2 forbids this header, so the route does not set it on HTTP/2.

The new tests use raw keep-alive sockets. They check that the server closes
the socket after each failure, and that a successful upload keeps the
connection usable. Also clear the timer in the first Azure abort test.
